The longest journey

Every year, a small grey and white seabird completes what is thought to be the longest migration of any animal on Earth. The Arctic tern breeds in the far north, in places such as Greenland, Iceland and northern Canada, during the brief Arctic summer. When the breeding season ends, it flies south, past the coasts of Europe and Africa or South America, all the way to the edge of Antarctica, where it spends the southern summer. Then it returns north again to breed.

For a long time, scientists could only estimate the length of this journey. Birds were fitted with small metal rings on their legs, and occasionally a ringed bird would be found thousands of kilometres from where it had been ringed. These records proved that terns travelled between the two polar regions, but they revealed little about the routes the birds took or how long the journey lasted.

The picture changed when researchers began to use tiny tracking devices called geolocators. These devices, which weigh less than two grams, record the amount of daylight at regular intervals. From the times of sunrise and sunset, scientists can calculate the approximate position of the bird each day. In one study, geolocators were attached to a group of terns breeding in Greenland and Iceland. Because the devices store their data rather than transmitting it, they can only be read once they have been removed from the bird. When the birds returned a year later and the devices were recovered, the results were astonishing. The average distance travelled during the year was around 70,000 kilometres, and some individuals covered considerably more.

The study also showed that the terns do not fly directly from north to south. Instead, they follow a route shaped roughly like the letter S across the Atlantic. This appears to allow them to take advantage of the prevailing winds, which means they use less energy than they would if they flew in a straight line. The tracking data also revealed that, on the southward journey, most of the birds stopped for several weeks in an area of the North Atlantic, far from land, where cold water rises from the deep sea and brings with it large amounts of food. Here the birds were able to build up the reserves of fat they would need for the rest of the journey. On the return flight in spring, by contrast, the terns travelled much faster and made fewer stops, possibly because arriving early at the breeding grounds gives a bird a better chance of securing a good nesting site. The northward journey took, on average, about forty days, compared with around ninety days for the journey south.

The Arctic tern is not a large bird. An adult weighs only about a hundred grams, less than a typical mobile phone. It is, however, extremely long-lived for a bird of its size, and individuals are known to have survived for more than thirty years. Over such a lifetime, a tern may fly a total distance equivalent to travelling to the Moon and back three times.

Because it spends the summer in the Arctic and then a second summer in the Antarctic, the Arctic tern experiences more daylight than any other animal. This is useful, because the tern feeds by sight. It hovers above the water, looking for small fish and shrimp-like animals near the surface, and then dives to catch them. Long hours of daylight mean long hours of feeding.

Arctic terns nest in colonies, often on small islands or along stony beaches, where they lay their eggs directly on the ground with little or no nest material. The eggs are well camouflaged, which protects them from some predators, but the adults also defend their nests aggressively. Anyone who walks too close to a colony is likely to be attacked from the air, and the birds frequently strike intruders on the head with their sharp beaks. Experienced visitors to tern colonies often wear a hat or carry a stick above their heads, because the birds tend to aim at the highest point.

Although the Arctic tern is not currently considered to be in danger, scientists are watching it closely. Because it depends on the conditions at both ends of the Earth and at several points in between, it may be particularly sensitive to changes in the environment. In some breeding colonies, a shortage of the small fish that terns feed their chicks has led to years in which very few young birds survived. Researchers hope that the tracking studies, which are now being carried out at colonies in several countries, will help to identify the places along the route that matter most to the birds, so that these areas can be protected.

Ice before refrigerators

Today, ice is something most people can make in their own kitchens without thinking about it. But for most of human history, ice in warm weather was a rare luxury, and keeping it from melting required considerable effort and ingenuity.

The earliest known methods of storing ice come from dry, hot regions. In parts of ancient Persia, people built large domed structures above deep pits. In winter, water was channelled into shallow pools beside the structure, where it froze during the cold desert nights. The ice was then cut and placed in the pit, which was insulated by thick walls made of a special mixture of clay, sand and other materials. Ice stored in this way could last through the hot summer months and was used to cool drinks and to make chilled desserts. Some of these structures were large enough to hold thousands of cubic metres of ice, and a few of them can still be seen today.

The idea of keeping winter ice for summer use was not limited to Persia. Records from ancient China describe ice being collected from rivers and stored in cellars, and in parts of the Mediterranean, snow was carried down from the mountains and kept in pits covered with branches and leaves. In each case, the basic principle was the same: ice melts more slowly when it is kept in large quantities, away from sunlight and protected from warm air.


In Europe, the use of ice houses became widespread among wealthy landowners in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. A typical ice house was a brick chamber, often shaped like an egg, built partly or wholly underground. It was usually placed on a north-facing slope or among trees, where it would receive as little sun as possible. In winter, workers cut blocks of ice from frozen lakes and ponds on the estate and carried them to the ice house, where they were packed tightly together. Layers of straw were placed between and around the blocks to provide insulation. A drain at the bottom carried away the water from any ice that did melt, since standing water would cause the rest of the ice to melt more quickly.

A well-built ice house could keep ice for a year or even longer. The ice was used in the kitchen to preserve food such as fish and meat, to make ice cream, which was a fashionable dessert among the rich, and sometimes for medical purposes, for instance to reduce a patient's fever. For the people who owned them, ice houses were also a symbol of wealth, since only a large estate could afford the labour needed to fill one.

In the nineteenth century, ice became a commercial product on a huge scale. Merchants in the north-east of the United States discovered that ice cut from frozen lakes in winter could be shipped to hot countries, packed in sawdust, and still arrive in usable condition. At first, many people thought the idea was ridiculous, and early shipments lost money. But the trade grew rapidly, and ice was eventually exported to the Caribbean, South America and even India, a voyage that took several months.

Britain, too, imported large quantities of natural ice, much of it from Norway, where the cold climate and the many lakes close to the coast made it easy to harvest and transport. The ice arrived by ship and was stored in enormous ice wells, some of them more than ten metres deep, before being delivered to fishmongers, restaurants and private homes. In cities, ice was sold from carts, and households that could afford it kept a wooden cabinet lined with metal, known as an icebox, in which a block of ice kept food cool for a day or two.

The natural ice trade had its problems, however. A mild winter could mean that there was not enough ice to harvest, and prices rose sharply. There were also growing concerns about cleanliness, because ice taken from lakes and rivers might contain dirt or be contaminated by waste. These concerns encouraged the development of machines that could produce ice artificially from clean water. The first such machines appeared in the middle of the nineteenth century, and by the early twentieth century, factory-made ice had largely replaced natural ice in most industrialised countries.

The final step was the arrival of the electric refrigerator in ordinary homes, which happened gradually during the twentieth century. With it, the need for ice houses, ice ships and ice carts disappeared. Many of the old ice houses still survive on country estates, but most are now empty. Some have found an unexpected new role: their cool, dark and stable conditions make them ideal places for bats to spend the winter, and conservation groups have adapted several of them for this purpose.

Lights on the coast

For as long as people have travelled by sea, the point at which the sea meets the land has been the most dangerous part of any voyage. Rocks hidden just below the surface, sandbanks that shift with every storm and headlands that are invisible at night have wrecked countless ships. The earliest attempts to warn sailors were simple: fires were lit on hilltops or on the roofs of tall buildings near harbours. These fires burned wood, and later coal, and they had to be fed by hand throughout the night. On a windy night a fire might consume several tonnes of fuel, and in heavy rain it could go out altogether, just when it was most needed.

For centuries, progress was slow. By the eighteenth century, many towers used candles or oil lamps instead of open fires, but the light they produced was weak and spread in all directions, so that most of it was wasted on the sky and the land. Glass windows protected the flames from the wind, but they quickly became covered in soot, and keepers had to clean them several times a night. A ship's captain could often see a coal fire from further away than one of these early lamps.

The first great improvement came with the use of curved mirrors. A polished metal reflector placed behind a lamp collected the light that would otherwise have been lost and sent it out towards the sea in a single beam. Towers were soon fitted with dozens of lamps, each with its own reflector, and their range increased dramatically. The mirrors, however, were made of copper coated with silver, and they lost their shine within a few months, so they had to be polished constantly.

The most important breakthrough came in the 1820s, when a French engineer designed a new kind of lens. Instead of a single thick piece of glass, which would have been extremely heavy and would have absorbed much of the light, his lens was made up of many separate rings of glass arranged around a central lamp. Each ring bent the light slightly, and together they focused it into a powerful horizontal beam. A lens of this type could send light more than thirty kilometres, and because it lost far less light than a mirror, it needed only a single lamp. Within a few decades, lenses of this design had been installed in lighthouses around the world, and some are still in use today.

A lighthouse that simply shone all night had one serious weakness: sailors could not always tell which lighthouse they were looking at. The solution was to give each one a unique pattern, known as its character. Some lights flashed once every few seconds; others flashed in groups of two or three, or showed a steady light that went dark at intervals. To produce these patterns, the lens was mounted on a platform that turned slowly, driven by a clockwork mechanism powered by a heavy weight. The weight had to be wound back to the top of the tower by hand every few hours. To reduce friction, the largest lenses floated on a bath of mercury, which allowed several tonnes of glass to be turned by the gentle push of one hand.

Life for the keepers was demanding and often lonely. Many lighthouses stood on small islands or isolated rocks, and the keepers might not see their families for weeks at a time. Their duties were strictly defined: they trimmed the wicks, cleaned the lens, wound the clockwork and recorded the weather in a logbook. On stations where fog was common, they also operated a foghorn, since a light, however powerful, cannot be seen through thick fog. Supplies arrived by boat, and in bad weather a station could be cut off for a month or more.

During the twentieth century, electricity transformed the lighthouse. Electric lamps were brighter and more reliable than oil, and they could be switched on and off automatically. Gradually, the role of the keeper disappeared. Lights were controlled first from nearby stations and later from a central office many kilometres away, and the last keepers in many countries left their towers in the 1990s. Today, a typical lighthouse is visited only occasionally by engineers who check the equipment.

Some people have asked whether lighthouses are needed at all, now that almost every ship carries satellite navigation. Most maritime authorities, however, believe they still have a role. Electronic systems can fail, and small boats, such as those used by fishermen and people sailing on holiday, do not always carry the latest equipment. A light on a headland is also a simple way of confirming what a screen is showing. As a result, although some minor lights have been switched off, the majority continue to operate. Many of the keepers' cottages, meanwhile, have found a new purpose as holiday homes or small museums, attracting visitors who want to experience, at least for a few nights, the isolation that the keepers once knew.

sets.passage:
The dance of the honey bee

A honey bee colony can contain as many as fifty thousand individuals, but only a small proportion of them ever leave the hive to collect food. These foragers face a difficult task. The flowers that provide nectar and pollen may be several kilometres away, they bloom for only a few days or weeks, and their location changes constantly through the season. A colony that relied on each forager to find flowers by chance would quickly starve. Instead, honey bees have developed one of the most remarkable communication systems in the animal world: a dance that tells other bees where food can be found.

The dance takes place in the darkness of the hive, on the vertical surface of the wax comb. A forager that has discovered a rich source of food returns home and begins to move in a figure-of-eight pattern. In the middle section of the figure, she walks in a straight line while shaking her body rapidly from side to side, a movement known as the waggle. She then circles back, first to one side and then to the other, and repeats the straight run. Other bees crowd around her, following her movements closely and touching her with their antennae.

The information is contained in two features of the straight run. The first is its direction. Because the comb is vertical, the dancer uses gravity as a reference point: a run straight up the comb means that the food lies in the direction of the sun, while a run at an angle of, say, forty degrees to the right of vertical means that the food lies forty degrees to the right of the sun. The second feature is the length of the run. The longer the waggle lasts, the further away the food is. Roughly speaking, each second of waggling represents about a kilometre of flight, although the exact relationship varies between different populations of bees.

Scientists began to decode the dance in the first half of the twentieth century, and their conclusions were not immediately accepted. Some researchers argued that bees found food mainly by smell, following the scent of flowers carried on the dancer's body. The debate was settled only in the early 2000s, when experiments using radar to track individual bees showed that recruits flew directly towards the area indicated by the dance, even when the scent of the flowers had been removed. Smell, it turned out, helped bees to locate the exact flowers once they had reached the right area, but the dance told them where to go.

There is a further complication. The sun moves across the sky during the day, so a dance that pointed correctly at nine in the morning would be wrong by noon. Remarkably, bees take this into account. A forager that dances for a long period gradually changes the angle of her run to match the movement of the sun, even though she cannot see it from inside the hive. On cloudy days, bees can still navigate because they are able to detect patterns of polarised light in the sky that are invisible to humans.

Not every dance is equally enthusiastic. A bee that has found a particularly rich source, with plenty of sweet nectar close to the hive, repeats her dance many more times than one that has found a poor source, so that more recruits are sent to the better location. In this way, the colony as a whole is able to direct its workforce towards the most profitable flowers without any single bee comparing the options. Researchers have compared this process to the way markets distribute resources, with no central authority making decisions.

The dance is also used for a quite different purpose. In late spring, when a colony becomes too large, the old queen leaves with around half of the workers to establish a new home. The swarm gathers on a branch while scout bees search for a suitable hollow, such as a gap in a tree. When a scout finds a promising site, she returns and dances to advertise it. Over a period of hours or days, more and more scouts visit the most popular sites, until one location attracts a clear majority. Only then does the whole swarm take off.

Understanding the dance has practical value. Scientists have begun to record dances in hives placed in towns and in the countryside, and to translate them into maps showing where bees are finding food in each month of the year. These maps have revealed some surprises: in several studies, bees in urban areas travelled shorter distances than those on farmland, suggesting that gardens may offer a richer supply of flowers than fields of a single crop. Such findings could help land managers decide where planting wild flowers would be most beneficial.

sets.passage:
The rise and fall of the canals

Before the age of railways, moving heavy goods overland was slow, expensive and often damaging to the goods themselves. Roads in eighteenth-century Britain were frequently little more than muddy tracks, and a horse pulling a cart could manage a load of perhaps a tonne. Coal, which was needed in ever greater quantities by the growing towns and factories, cost far more to transport than to dig out of the ground. Rivers offered an alternative, but many were too shallow, too winding or too fast to be used by boats, and they rarely passed close to where the coal was mined.

The answer was the canal: an artificial waterway built specifically for transport. On calm, still water, a single horse walking along a towpath beside the canal could pull a boat carrying around thirty tonnes, many times what it could pull on a road. The first canals of the industrial era were built in the 1760s to carry coal from mines to nearby towns, and their effect on prices was immediate. In one town, the price of coal is reported to have fallen by half within a year of the canal opening. Investors took notice, and over the following decades thousands of kilometres of canals were dug across the country, in what became known as a period of 'canal mania'.

Building a canal was an enormous undertaking. Almost all the work was done by hand, by teams of labourers who moved earth with spades and wheelbarrows. Because water must be level, engineers tried wherever possible to follow the natural contours of the land, which is why many canals wind back and forth across hillsides. Where a change in height could not be avoided, they built locks: chambers with gates at each end, in which the water level could be raised or lowered so that boats could move from one level to another. On steep slopes, dozens of locks might be built close together in a flight, and a boat could take several hours to pass through them.

Water supply was a constant concern. Every time a boat passed through a lock, a large quantity of water flowed down from the higher level, and this had to be replaced. Reservoirs were built in the hills to feed the highest sections, and in dry summers some canals had to close or limit the number of boats. Leaks were another problem. To make the bed of the canal watertight, workers lined it with a layer of clay mixed with water, which was trodden down until it formed a waterproof seal, a technique known as puddling.

For a few decades, canals were the most important freight network in the country. But their success was short-lived. From the 1830s, railways began to spread rapidly, and they offered something canals could not: speed. A train could cover in an hour a distance that took a canal boat a day. Many canal companies cut their prices in an attempt to compete, and some were bought by railway companies, which then allowed them to decline. By the early twentieth century, the remaining canal traffic consisted mainly of heavy, low-value goods such as coal and stone, for which speed mattered less than cost.

The families who worked the boats lived difficult lives. As earnings fell, many could no longer afford a house on land, and whole families lived in the tiny cabin at the back of the boat, which might measure only around three metres by two. Children often worked from an early age, leading the horse or operating the locks, and many received little formal education because they were constantly on the move.

By the middle of the twentieth century, commercial traffic had almost disappeared, and many canals became overgrown or were filled in. Their revival began in the 1950s and 1960s, when groups of volunteers began to clear rubbish, repair locks and campaign for the waterways to be reopened. Their argument was that the canals had value not for freight but for leisure. This proved correct. Today, the canals of Britain are used by tens of thousands of boats, almost all of them for holidays or as permanent homes, and the towpaths are popular with walkers, runners and cyclists.

The canals are now recognised as an important part of the country's history and environment. Many of the original bridges, tunnels and lock-keepers' cottages are protected buildings, and the water supports a wide range of wildlife, from fish and water birds to otters, which have returned to several waterways in recent years. Some engineers have even suggested that canals could be used again to carry goods, since a boat produces far less pollution per tonne than a lorry, although so far such schemes have been small in scale.

When the desert blooms

Deserts are usually imagined as places where almost nothing grows: vast areas of sand and rock, baked by the sun and swept by dry winds. Yet in certain years, some deserts are transformed. After unusually heavy rain, the ground can become covered within weeks by millions of flowers, turning brown landscapes yellow, purple and white. These events, sometimes called superblooms, usually occur only about once in a decade, and they attract large numbers of visitors who travel long distances to see them. In some towns near the edge of the desert, the arrival of the flowers has become a reason for local celebrations.

The plants responsible are mostly annuals, species that complete their entire life cycle, from seed to flower to seed again, within a single season. In a desert, this strategy has a clear advantage. Rather than trying to survive the long dry periods as living plants, which would require deep roots, thick leaves or other costly adaptations, annuals spend most of their existence as seeds lying in the soil. Some of these plants are so small that they are easy to overlook even when they are in flower, while others grow to the height of a person within a few weeks. A seed needs almost no water and can remain alive for many years, waiting for the right conditions.

Waiting, however, carries its own risks. If a seed germinates after a light shower, the young plant may die before it can produce seeds of its own, because the soil dries out too quickly. Many desert annuals have therefore evolved mechanisms that prevent them from germinating unless there has been enough rain. Some seeds have a coating containing chemicals that stop germination; only a heavy downpour can wash these chemicals away. Others respond to temperature as well as moisture, so that they germinate only after rain at a particular time of year, when the following weeks are likely to be cool enough for the plants to grow.

Even in a good year, not every seed responds. Studies of desert soils have shown that a significant proportion of seeds remain dormant after heavy rain, while others in the same patch of ground germinate. Biologists believe that this is a form of insurance. If all the seeds germinated at once and the rains then failed, the population could be wiped out. By keeping some seeds in reserve, a species spreads its risk across many years, in much the same way that a careful investor avoids putting all of their money into a single company.

The timing of the rain is crucial. A superbloom generally requires a series of storms, rather than one, spread over the autumn and winter months, so that the soil stays moist for long enough. Temperature matters too: if the weeks after germination are very hot, the young plants dry out; if there is frost, they may be killed. Wind can also cause damage, drying the soil and sometimes burying seedlings under sand. For all these reasons, scientists find it difficult to predict a superbloom more than a few weeks in advance.

A bloom has effects that go far beyond the plants themselves. Insects that feed on nectar appear in huge numbers, among them bees, butterflies and moths, many of which also spend most of their lives in a dormant state. Some moths, for instance, remain in the soil as pupae for several years and emerge only when the flowers appear. Birds and lizards feed on the insects, and small mammals collect the new seeds and store them underground, where some are forgotten and later germinate. In this way, a single wet winter can support the desert food chain for several years afterwards.

The popularity of superblooms has created problems, however. In some areas, the number of visitors has been so great that roads have become blocked and fields of flowers have been damaged by people walking through them to take photographs. Because the soil in deserts is often covered by a fragile crust formed by tiny organisms, a single footprint can leave a mark that lasts for years. Park managers have responded by creating marked paths, limiting parking and, in a few places, temporarily closing the most popular sites.

Changes in the climate add a further uncertainty. Many climate models suggest that rainfall in desert regions will become more variable, with longer droughts broken by occasional intense storms. It is not yet clear what this will mean for desert annuals. Heavy rain might trigger more frequent blooms, but longer droughts could exhaust the supply of seeds in the soil. For now, scientists are collecting seeds from many desert species and storing them in seed banks, so that populations can be restored if they decline.

sets.passage:
The problem with sitting

A
The average office worker now spends around ten hours a day sitting down: at a desk, in a car or on a train, and then on a sofa at home. Concern about the health effects of this has grown steadily over the past two decades, but the basic idea is not new. In the 1950s, researchers compared the drivers of double-decker buses, who sat for almost their entire shift, with the conductors, who climbed up and down the stairs hundreds of times a day collecting fares. The conductors had significantly fewer heart problems than the drivers, even though the two groups came from similar backgrounds and earned similar wages.

B
Why should sitting be harmful? Part of the answer lies in what happens inside our muscles. When we stand or move, the large muscles of the legs and back are constantly working, and in doing so they take fats and sugars out of the blood and use them as fuel. When we sit still for long periods, these muscles are largely inactive, and the body becomes less efficient at processing what we eat. It was once assumed that a daily run or a visit to the gym would cancel out these effects. Unfortunately, that assumption now looks too optimistic. Several large studies have found that people who exercise regularly but sit for most of the rest of the day still face higher health risks than those who move more throughout the day.

C
One difficulty for researchers is that sitting is surprisingly hard to measure. For many years, most studies relied on questionnaires in which people were asked to estimate how many hours they spent sitting. The trouble is that sitting is so routine that people rarely notice it, and studies comparing questionnaires with measurements have found that people underestimate their sitting time by as much as two hours a day. More recent research has used small sensors attached to the thigh, which record the angle of the leg every few seconds. In my view, these devices have done more than anything else to put the research on a reliable footing.

D
The most visible response to the research has been the spread of standing desks, which can be raised so that the user works on their feet. In some offices they have become almost a status symbol, and manufacturers now offer models that can be adjusted at the touch of a button. Prices have fallen considerably, and a basic frame that converts an ordinary desk into a standing one can now be bought for less than the cost of a good office chair. Yet standing all day is not the answer either. Workers in jobs that require long periods of standing, such as shop assistants, often suffer from pain in the legs and feet, as well as problems with the veins in their legs. Most specialists now recommend that people should change position regularly, rather than replacing one fixed posture with another.

E
How well do standing desks work in practice? One study followed the staff of an insurance company, half of whom were given adjustable desks. After six months, those with the new desks were sitting for about an hour less each day than their colleagues. However, the initial enthusiasm did not last. By the end of the year, many had returned to their old habits and kept their desks permanently in the lowered position. Interestingly, the employees who continued to use their desks were mostly those who had been sent regular reminders by a piece of software on their computers. It would be wrong to conclude that standing desks are useless, but they clearly need support if they are to change behaviour.

F
An alternative approach focuses on breaking up sitting time rather than replacing it. In laboratory experiments, volunteers who got up and walked for two or three minutes every half hour had lower levels of glucose in their blood after a meal than volunteers who sat continuously, and, more surprisingly, than volunteers who took a single thirty-minute walk. Short, frequent breaks, it seems, may matter more than the total amount of activity.

G
Ultimately, the problem may be as much cultural as physical. In many workplaces, sitting at a desk is seen as a sign of hard work, and an employee who keeps standing up may be regarded as restless or distracted. Changing this requires leadership. When managers themselves take regular breaks, hold short meetings standing up or suggest discussing a problem while walking, their staff are far more likely to follow. Some firms have introduced walking meetings for small groups, and standing meetings tend to be shorter. None of these changes is dramatic, but together they suggest that the solution to the problem of sitting lies not in expensive furniture but in the way we organise our working day.

sets.passage:
Tiny forests

A
On a strip of unused land beside a busy road, a group of volunteers is planting trees. But this is not an ordinary planting scheme. Within a space no larger than a tennis court, they will plant around six hundred young trees and shrubs, packed far more closely than in any park. The result, its supporters say, will be a 'tiny forest': a dense patch of woodland that will grow quickly, attract wildlife and need no care at all within a few years. The technique was developed in Japan in the 1970s by a botanist who had studied the small areas of ancient woodland that survived around temples and shrines. Over the past decade, it has spread to cities across Europe, Asia and North America, where it has been taken up by local councils, schools and environmental charities, and in some places by property developers keen to improve the image of new housing schemes.

B
The method follows a strict set of steps. First, the ground is dug to a depth of about a metre, and the soil is improved with large quantities of organic material, such as straw, compost and manure, so that the young roots can grow easily. Next, a mixture of native species is chosen, usually around thirty different kinds, ranging from tall trees to low shrubs, so that every layer of a natural forest is represented. These are then planted at a density of about three per square metre. For the first two or three years, volunteers water the site in dry weather and remove weeds. After that, no further maintenance is needed, and the forest is left to develop on its own.

C
The claims made for tiny forests are impressive. They are said to grow ten times faster than forests planted in the conventional way and to become thirty times denser. Such figures appear frequently on the websites of organisations that promote the method. However, they have rarely been tested in properly designed studies, and some ecologists point out that they seem to be based on a small number of early projects whose conditions may not be typical. Others note that growth rates depend heavily on climate, rainfall and the original quality of the soil, all of which vary enormously from one city to another, so a single figure for all sites is unlikely to be meaningful.

D
Some independent evidence is now beginning to appear. One study examined eleven tiny forests in a European country, two years after they had been planted, and compared them with nearby areas of grassland and parkland. The researchers recorded over six hundred species of insects and other small animals in the forests, many more than in the comparison sites. Bird and mammal numbers, on the other hand, were low, which is perhaps not surprising: a forest the size of a tennis court is simply too small to provide a home for larger animals.

E
For many supporters, the social benefits are just as important as the ecological ones. Local schools are often involved from the beginning, and children help to prepare the ground and plant the trees. Some schools use their forest as an outdoor classroom, measuring the growth of the trees and counting the insects that visit. Organisers say that when local people have helped to create a forest, they feel a sense of ownership, and that sites planted by the community suffer much less damage than those planted by contractors. Planting days often attract families who have never met their neighbours before, and in several cities volunteer groups that formed to plant a forest have gone on to organise other local projects, from litter collections to community gardens.

F
Not everyone is convinced. Because of the deep digging and the large amount of organic material required, a tiny forest costs considerably more per square metre to create than a conventional woodland. Critics also point out that, at such high densities, many of the young trees will inevitably die as they compete for light. Supporters reply that this is exactly what happens in a natural forest. There is also a question about the name itself. Calling a small group of trees a forest may give people a false impression of what has been achieved, and could even be used by developers to justify cutting down real woodland elsewhere.

G
Tiny forests are clearly not a substitute for protecting large areas of existing forest, and nobody seriously suggests that they are. Their value lies elsewhere. In crowded urban neighbourhoods, where there is no room for a park, a tiny forest may be the only realistic way of bringing nature closer to people's homes. If the method's supporters can be persuaded to describe its benefits more modestly, and if more careful research is carried out, tiny forests may well find a lasting place in the cities of the future.

sets.passage:
Working less, achieving more?

A
Not long ago, the idea of a four-day working week belonged on the fringes of economic debate. Today it is discussed by governments, trade unions and business leaders, and hundreds of companies around the world have tried it. The version that has attracted most attention is often summarised as '100-80-100': employees receive 100 per cent of their pay for working 80 per cent of their previous hours, in return for a commitment to maintain 100 per cent of their productivity.

B
It is easy to forget that the five-day week is itself a relatively recent invention. For much of the nineteenth century, factory workers commonly worked six days a week, often for ten hours or more a day. In the early twentieth century, some employers began to reduce working hours, arguing that rested workers made fewer mistakes and produced more. These early experiments were often met with scepticism from other business owners, who feared that shorter hours would simply mean less output. In many cases, however, output held steady or even increased, partly because tired workers had been responsible for costly errors and accidents. Gradually, trade unions and governments took up the cause, and by the middle of the century the two-day weekend had become normal in many industrialised countries. In 1930, one well-known economist even predicted that, thanks to rising productivity, his grandchildren's generation would need to work only fifteen hours a week. That prediction, to put it mildly, has not been fulfilled.

C
Most recent trials have followed a similar pattern. Companies volunteer to take part, and they are given several months to prepare, during which managers and staff look for ways to remove unnecessary tasks, such as long meetings and excessive emails. The trial itself usually lasts six months. Throughout this period, researchers collect information on the company's revenue, the number of days staff are absent and the rate at which employees leave. Staff also complete regular surveys about their stress levels, sleep and satisfaction with their work. In some trials, these surveys continue for a further six months after the trial has ended, so that researchers can see whether any benefits last once the novelty has worn off.

D
The results have generally been encouraging. In one large trial involving around sixty companies, the great majority decided to continue the shorter week after the trial had ended, and only a handful returned to their previous arrangements. Employees reported significantly lower levels of burnout, and the number of sick days fell by around two thirds. Revenue, meanwhile, remained broadly stable, and in some cases it rose slightly. Many staff said they used their extra day for household tasks and appointments, which freed up the weekend for rest and family life. Managers, too, reported advantages: several said that it had become easier to attract applicants for job vacancies, since a shorter week was seen as a valuable benefit by people looking for work.

E
These findings need to be treated with some caution, however. The companies that volunteer for trials are, almost by definition, those whose managers already believe the idea might work, and they are likely to make greater efforts to ensure its success. Most of them are also small, office-based businesses, where productivity is relatively easy to maintain by cutting meetings. It is much less clear how a four-day week would work in hospitals, schools or shops, where the service depends on staff being physically present. This does not mean the findings are worthless, but it does mean they cannot simply be applied to every employer.

F
It is also important to recognise that the 'four-day week' can mean different things. In some companies, staff work the same total number of hours as before, but over four longer days. This compressed arrangement saves time spent travelling to work, but long days can lead to fatigue, and some studies suggest that productivity falls in the final hours of a long shift. Other companies reduce total hours but stagger the days off, so that some staff take Monday off and others Friday, allowing the business to stay open five days a week.

G
Several governments are now funding further trials, including a small number in public services such as local councils, where the challenges described above are particularly acute. Some are also considering whether the law should give workers the right to request a shorter week. It seems unlikely that the four-day week will become standard across the economy in the near future; the obstacles in many sectors are simply too great. What does seem likely is that the trials will continue to change expectations, and that employers who refuse to discuss more flexible working patterns of any kind may find it increasingly difficult to recruit staff.

sets.passage:
Keeping languages alive

A
Linguists estimate that around seven thousand languages are spoken in the world today, and that nearly half of them are endangered. Many have only a few hundred speakers, and some have only a handful, most of them elderly. The problem is not evenly spread: some regions of the world contain a remarkable number of languages within a small area, and it is often in exactly these places that the pressure on smaller languages is greatest. A language is generally considered to be at risk not when the number of speakers falls below a particular figure, but when children stop learning it at home. Once that happens, the language may continue to be spoken for decades, but unless something changes, it will eventually disappear with its last speakers.

B
In the past, minority languages were sometimes actively suppressed, and children were punished for speaking them at school. Today, the pressures are usually less direct, but they can be just as powerful. As families move to cities in search of work, they find themselves surrounded by a dominant national or international language. Schooling, television and the internet are mostly in that language, and so are the jobs that offer the best pay. Marriage between speakers of different languages can also play a part, since couples often adopt a shared language at home, which is usually the dominant one. Many parents therefore decide, quite reasonably, that their children's future lies in the dominant language, and stop using their own at home. In most cases, then, the decline of a language today results not from force but from the choices of individual families.

C
Why should this matter? One reason is that languages contain knowledge that may not exist anywhere else. Communities that have lived in one place for many generations often have detailed vocabularies for local plants, animals and weather. In some languages, for example, there are separate words for dozens of varieties of a single plant, reflecting differences in taste, medicinal use or the time of year when it can be harvested. When the language goes, this information can easily be lost too, since it is rarely written down. For speakers themselves, a language is also closely tied to identity, to songs and stories, and to a sense of belonging.

D
Over the past forty years, a number of approaches have been developed to reverse the decline. One of the best known is the 'language nest', first set up in New Zealand in the early 1980s. Language nests are preschools in which older speakers look after very young children entirely in the endangered language. Because children of that age learn languages quickly and naturally, the approach can produce fluent speakers within a few years. Parents are often encouraged to attend classes themselves, so that the language can be used at home as well as at the nest. The model has since been adopted by communities in several other countries, often with the help of local volunteers, although finding enough older speakers with the time and energy to work with small children every day is a constant challenge.


E
Where there are very few speakers left, a different method may be needed. In master-apprentice programmes, a fluent speaker, usually an older person, is paired with a single adult learner. The two spend between ten and twenty hours a week together, cooking, gardening, shopping or simply talking, and they agree to use only the endangered language throughout. The emphasis is on everyday communication rather than grammar lessons, and many learners reach a good level of fluency within three years.

F
Technology also has a role to play. Online dictionaries, recordings of elderly speakers, mobile apps and social media groups have all made it easier for learners, especially young people who live far from their community, to hear and use a language. Some communities have also produced children's cartoons, songs and even video games in their languages, giving young people a reason to use them for entertainment as well as for study.
 However, technology on its own cannot create new speakers. An app may teach vocabulary, but a language survives only if people use it with one another in daily life.

G
There are reasons for optimism. Some languages that seemed to be in serious decline only a few generations ago have stabilised, or even grown, thanks to bilingual schooling, broadcasting and official recognition. Welsh, for example, is now taught to every child in Wales, and the number of young speakers has increased. Yet the experience of such languages also shows that success does not depend mainly on money or technology. What matters most is the determination of the community itself to keep speaking its language, and to make sure that the next generation does the same.

sets.passage:
Learning from mistakes

A
For much of the twentieth century, mistakes had a poor reputation in education. Many teachers believed that if students were allowed to give wrong answers, those answers would become fixed in their memories and be difficult to remove. Lessons were therefore designed to keep errors to a minimum. New material was introduced in small steps, students were given plenty of hints, and they were tested only when they were almost certain to succeed. This approach, sometimes called errorless learning, still has its place, particularly for people with certain memory difficulties. But over the past twenty years, a growing body of research has suggested that, for most learners, making mistakes may be an important part of learning rather than an obstacle to it.

B
Some of the most striking evidence comes from studies of what psychologists call pretesting. In a typical experiment, two groups of students study the same text. One group simply reads it. The other is first asked questions about the content, questions they cannot possibly answer correctly, since they have not yet seen the material. When both groups are tested later, the students who guessed, and usually guessed wrong, tend to remember more. Similar results have been found with learners of all ages, from primary school children to adults on professional courses. The most widely accepted explanation is that an attempt to answer, even an unsuccessful one, prepares the mind to notice the correct information when it appears. The learner has, in effect, created a space that the answer then fills.

C
A related finding concerns confidence. It might be expected that the mistakes people make with great confidence would be the hardest to correct, because the learner is so sure of the wrong answer. In fact, the opposite appears to be true. When people discover that an answer they were certain about is wrong, they are more likely to remember the correction than when they discover that a mere guess was wrong. Researchers believe that the surprise of being wrong captures attention and makes the moment more memorable. This has been named the hypercorrection effect.

D
None of this means that every mistake is helpful. The benefits depend heavily on what happens next. If learners are not told the right answer, or are told it only after a long delay, the error itself may be what they remember. In one study of adults learning vocabulary in a foreign language, participants who received feedback immediately after each wrong guess performed far better than those who received it the following day. Feedback also needs to be specific: simply telling a learner that an answer is wrong, without showing why, is of limited value.

E
There is also an emotional dimension. Many students, especially older ones, are deeply anxious about being seen to fail, and this anxiety can make them reluctant to attempt difficult questions at all. Some teachers have tried to change this by making errors a normal part of classroom discussion. One secondary school mathematics teacher, for instance, collects wrong answers from a test, removes the names, and asks the class to work out where each one went wrong. Her students report that the exercise has made them less afraid of making mistakes themselves, and several say they now find it easier to ask questions in class. Other teachers give credit for the quality of an attempt as well as for the final answer.

F
The idea that mistakes can be valuable is not limited to schools. In industries where errors can have serious consequences, such as aviation and healthcare, organisations have increasingly encouraged staff to report their own mistakes and near misses. The aim is not to punish individuals but to identify weaknesses in systems, such as confusing labels on medicines or unclear procedures, which might cause someone else to make the same mistake in future. Such schemes work only if employees trust that an honest report will not damage their careers, and building that trust can take many years.

G
It would be easy to draw the wrong lesson from this research. I am not suggesting that teachers should deliberately trick students into making mistakes, or that every error is a hidden opportunity. Some errors, particularly in practical subjects such as chemistry or engineering, can be dangerous, and others are simply the result of carelessness. Nevertheless, I believe the evidence is strong enough to justify a change in attitude. Students who are allowed to struggle with a problem, and who are given clear feedback when they get it wrong, are likely to understand it more deeply than those who are always guided to the right answer. Whether education systems that rely heavily on examinations will make room for this kind of struggle is another question.

sets.passage:
Losing the dark

A
Until little more than a century ago, night was genuinely dark for most of the world's population. Away from the light of a fire or a candle, people could see thousands of stars on a clear night, and the band of the Milky Way stretched across the sky. Today, according to estimates based on satellite images, more than eight out of ten people live under skies affected by artificial light, and for a large proportion of them the Milky Way is no longer visible at all. Astronomers were the first to raise concerns, since light from towns made it increasingly difficult to observe faint objects. But the problem, often described as light pollution, is now recognised as having consequences far beyond astronomy.

B
Light pollution takes several forms. The most familiar is skyglow, the orange or white dome that hangs over cities and can be seen from many kilometres away. It is caused by light that is directed upwards or sideways, either deliberately or through badly designed fittings, and is then scattered by particles in the atmosphere. Skyglow can affect places with no lights of their own, such as nature reserves many kilometres from the nearest town. Glare, the excessive brightness that makes it hard to see, is a second form, and is a particular hazard for drivers. A third is light trespass: light that spills into places where it is not wanted, such as through a bedroom window from a nearby street lamp.

C
For wildlife, the effects can be severe. Many animals rely on the natural pattern of light and darkness to regulate their behaviour. Young sea turtles, for example, find their way from the beach where they hatch to the ocean by moving towards the brightest horizon, which, under natural conditions, is the sea. On beaches near brightly lit roads and buildings, many crawl inland instead and die. Migrating birds that fly at night can be drawn towards lit buildings, and insects gather in vast numbers around street lamps, where many are eaten or die of exhaustion. Because insects pollinate plants and provide food for birds and bats, these losses can affect entire ecosystems. Even plants may respond: trees close to street lamps have been observed to keep their leaves later into the autumn than trees in darker areas.

D
Humans, too, may be affected. Our bodies have an internal clock that is set largely by exposure to light, and the hormone melatonin, which helps to regulate sleep, is produced mainly in darkness. Exposure to light at night can reduce the amount of melatonin the body produces. Several large studies have found associations between high levels of outdoor light at night and poorer sleep, although researchers caution that these studies cannot prove that light is the cause, since people who live in brightly lit areas may differ from others in many ways, such as the noise they are exposed to or the hours they work.

E
The arrival of LED street lights has complicated the picture. LEDs use far less electricity than older lamps, and many local authorities have replaced their lights to save money and reduce energy use. However, the first generation of LED street lights produced a cold, bluish-white light, which scatters more in the atmosphere than warmer colours and which has a stronger effect on the body's internal clock. In some places, the switch to LEDs was followed by complaints from residents and an increase in skyglow. More recent LED lights are available in warmer colours, and many authorities now choose these instead.

F
Unlike many environmental problems, light pollution is relatively easy to reduce. Shielded fittings that direct light only downwards can cut skyglow dramatically without making streets any darker at ground level. Lights can be dimmed late at night, when few people are about, or fitted with sensors so that they come on only when someone approaches. Several towns have experimented with switching off some street lights after midnight. Fears that this would lead to more accidents have so far not been supported by the evidence, although residents in some areas say that they feel less safe.

G
Some places have gone further, setting out to protect the night sky as a resource in its own right. A number of national parks and rural areas have been recognised as dark-sky reserves, where lighting is carefully controlled. As well as benefiting wildlife, these reserves have become an unexpected source of income: visitors travel to them specifically to see the stars, and local businesses offer guided observation evenings, often in winter, when there are few other tourists. For communities that depend on tourism, the dark has become something worth selling.

sets.passage:
Fixing things again

A
On the first Saturday of every month, a community hall in a small town fills with people carrying broken objects: a toaster that no longer heats, a lamp with a loose wire, a child's toy with a missing wheel, a jacket with a torn pocket. They have come to a repair café, an event at which volunteers with practical skills try to fix whatever is brought to them, free of charge, while the owners watch and, ideally, learn. Some visitors bring objects that have been in their families for generations; others arrive with something bought only months earlier. The first repair cafés appeared around fifteen years ago, and there are now thousands of them in dozens of countries. Their rapid spread says something about a growing unease with the way many products are made, used and thrown away.

B
For most of human history, repair was simply part of life. Clothes were mended until they could be mended no more, and furniture, tools and household goods were expected to last for decades. In the second half of the twentieth century, this changed. As manufacturing became cheaper, it often became less expensive to replace an item than to have it fixed, and the network of small repair shops that once existed in most towns gradually disappeared. At the same time, products became more complex, and the skills needed to repair them became more specialised.

C
Some critics go further, arguing that manufacturers deliberately design products to fail, a practice known as planned obsolescence. The evidence for this is mixed. There are well-documented historical cases in which manufacturers agreed among themselves to limit the life of their products, but in many modern cases a short lifespan seems to be the result of pressure to reduce costs rather than a deliberate plan. What is clearer is that many products are difficult to repair. Parts are glued rather than screwed together, batteries are sealed inside cases, and spare parts or repair manuals are often unavailable to the public.

D
The environmental case for repair is strong. A large share of the energy and materials associated with an electronic device such as a phone or laptop is used in manufacturing it, rather than in using it. Extending its life by even a year or two can therefore make a significant difference to its overall impact. Waste is another concern: discarded electronic goods are among the fastest-growing types of rubbish, and only a fraction of them are properly recycled. Many contain small quantities of valuable metals that are lost when they end up in landfill. Clothing tells a similar story: producing a single cotton shirt requires a large amount of water, yet many clothes are worn far fewer times than they could be.

E
Repair cafés themselves keep careful records. According to the data collected by one network, around six out of ten items brought in are successfully repaired, with the highest success rates for bicycles and clothing and the lowest for electronic items such as phones. Clothing repairs are often the quickest, and a skilled volunteer can replace a broken zip in less than half an hour. Volunteers report that the most common faults are surprisingly simple: a broken switch, a blocked filter or a loose connection. In many cases, owners had assumed that their item was beyond saving and had been about to throw it away.

F
The social side of the events is often mentioned by participants. Many volunteers are retired engineers, electricians or tailors who enjoy using their skills and passing them on, and visitors frequently say that they come as much for the conversation as for the repair. For some older residents, a repair café is one of the few regular opportunities to meet people from different generations. Organisers also see the events as a way of challenging the idea that only experts can understand how things work. Some cafés now run short workshops at which people can learn basic skills, such as sewing on a button or replacing a fuse in a plug.

G
It would be wrong, though, to exaggerate what repair cafés can achieve. They fix a few thousand items a month in a world that discards millions every day, and they depend on volunteers whose skills are not always being passed on to younger people. In my view, their greatest value lies not in the number of objects they save, but in the change in attitude they encourage. A person who has watched a kettle being opened and mended is less likely to see the next broken object as rubbish. If manufacturers can be persuaded to design products that are easier to open and repair, that change in attitude could matter a great deal.

sets.passage:
Can happiness be measured?

A
For most of the twentieth century, the success of a country was judged largely by economic measures, above all the total value of the goods and services it produced each year. Rising output was taken as a sign that people's lives were improving. Over the past few decades, however, a growing number of researchers have argued that such figures give an incomplete picture. Critics pointed out, for example, that money spent on treating illness or cleaning up pollution adds to economic output, even though nobody's life is better as a result. A country can become richer while its citizens become more stressed, more lonely or less healthy. These researchers have therefore tried to measure something more direct: how people themselves feel about their lives.

B
The most common method is remarkably simple. People are asked to rate their satisfaction with life as a whole on a scale, typically from nought to ten. Some surveys also ask more specific questions, for instance about how worthwhile people feel their daily activities are, or how anxious they felt on the previous day. Large surveys using questions of this kind are now carried out regularly in many countries, and the results are often published as league tables ranking nations from the happiest to the least happy. Such rankings attract a great deal of media attention, although the differences between countries near the middle of the tables are often too small to be meaningful.

C
Critics have raised a number of objections. One is that people in different cultures may interpret the questions differently. In some societies, it is considered boastful to describe oneself as very happy, while in others a cheerful answer is expected. Translation presents further difficulties, since words for happiness and satisfaction do not have exact equivalents in every language. Researchers have attempted to address these problems, for example by testing whether the same question produces similar answers when it is translated in different ways, but the issue has not been entirely resolved.

D
A second objection is that answers can be influenced by trivial circumstances. In one well-known type of experiment, people who were questioned on a sunny day reported higher satisfaction than those questioned when it was raining. Similarly, the order of questions matters: people who are first asked about their relationships or their health may give a different overall rating from those who are asked about their life as a whole at the start. Supporters of the surveys accept that individual answers are affected in this way, but they argue that such effects tend to cancel out when thousands of people are questioned.

E
Some researchers prefer a different approach, focusing not on how people judge their lives but on how they feel from moment to moment. In studies using this method, participants carry a phone that asks them at random times during the day what they are doing and how they feel. One advantage of this method is that it relies less on memory, since people describe how they feel at that moment rather than trying to sum up months or years. The results can be surprising. Activities that people say they value highly, such as looking after children, are not always associated with the most positive feelings at the time, while ordinary activities such as talking with friends score consistently well. Commuting, in contrast, regularly appears among the least enjoyable parts of the day.

F
What do the surveys reveal about the sources of wellbeing? Income matters, particularly for people who are poor, but beyond a certain level additional money appears to bring smaller and smaller gains. Health, both physical and mental, is strongly linked to life satisfaction, as is having secure work. Age plays a part too: perhaps surprisingly, older people often report higher life satisfaction than those in middle age. But the factors that stand out most consistently are social: having people to rely on in times of trouble, feeling trusted by others and spending time with friends and family. Unemployment, by contrast, has an effect on wellbeing that seems to be much larger than the loss of income alone would explain.

G
A number of countries now publish official measures of wellbeing alongside economic statistics, and some have begun to consider them when deciding how to spend public money. Supporters say this encourages decisions that improve people's lives rather than simply increase output. Sceptics worry that wellbeing figures are too easily influenced to be a reliable guide. Most researchers would probably agree that life satisfaction surveys are not a replacement for other statistics, but a useful addition to them, revealing aspects of life that economic figures alone cannot capture.

sets.passage:
In praise of the empty hour

Most of us now fill every spare moment. In a queue, on a bus or during the advertisements on television, we reach for our phones almost without thinking, and the slightest hint of boredom is dealt with before we have had time to notice it. In her new book, The Empty Hour, the psychologist Ruth Calloway argues that this is a mistake. Boredom, she claims, is not a problem to be solved but a signal worth listening to, and by eliminating it from our lives we may be losing something valuable. It is an appealing argument, and Calloway makes it with energy and considerable wit. Whether it entirely convinces is another matter.

The book opens with a brief history of boredom. Calloway points out that the word itself only came into common use in English in the nineteenth century, although the experience it describes is presumably much older. She suggests that the spread of factory work, with its repetitive tasks, and the growth of leisure time among the middle classes created new conditions in which people became conscious of being bored. This is an intriguing idea, but it is dealt with in barely twenty pages, and it rests on a handful of examples from novels and letters. Readers hoping for a serious historical account will be disappointed; this is the weakest part of the book.

Calloway is on firmer ground when she turns to her own field. Her central claim is that boredom has a function. It tells us, she argues, that what we are currently doing is not meeting our needs, and it pushes us to look for something more meaningful or interesting. To support this, she describes a series of experiments in which volunteers were first asked to carry out a deliberately tedious task, such as copying out long lists of numbers, and were then asked to think of as many uses as possible for an everyday object, such as a paper cup. In several of these studies, the volunteers who had been bored first came up with more original ideas than those who had not. Calloway presents these results as clear evidence that boredom stimulates creativity. Here some caution is needed. Most of the studies involved small numbers of participants, the effects they found were modest, and attempts to repeat them have produced mixed results. The findings are interesting, but they are not as conclusive as the book suggests.

The most persuasive chapter is the one on smartphones. Calloway's argument here is simple: phones relieve boredom so quickly and so efficiently that we never reach the point at which it might push us towards something more rewarding. She describes the phone as 'the snack that spoils the meal': a small, instant satisfaction that removes the hunger which would otherwise have led us to something more substantial. I confess that I recognised myself in this description. During the weeks I spent reading the book, I made a point of leaving my phone in my bag on train journeys, and found, somewhat to my surprise, that several ideas for my own work came to me while I was staring out of the window.

The final section of the book offers practical advice. Calloway recommends building what she calls 'empty time' into our lives: walking without headphones, waiting without a screen, and, for parents, resisting the temptation to fill every weekend with organised activities for their children, so that they have some unstructured time in which to invent their own games. Much of this is sensible, if hardly revolutionary, and some readers may feel they have heard it before. It is also worth noting that the advice seems to be aimed at a particular kind of reader. For a parent working long hours, or for someone caring for an elderly relative, the idea of deliberately setting aside empty time may seem less like wisdom than like a luxury.

To her credit, Calloway is aware of this. In the last chapter, she draws a distinction between boredom that is chosen and boredom that is imposed. The first, she argues, can be productive; the second, experienced for example by people in highly repetitive jobs or by prisoners, is often damaging and should not be romanticised. This distinction seems to me the most important idea in the book, and it is a pity that it appears so late. Had it been introduced at the beginning, it would have made many of the earlier arguments more precise, and it would have answered several of the objections that occurred to me as I was reading.

Calloway writes clearly and avoids unnecessary technical language, which will make the book accessible to a wide audience. She is fond of anecdotes from her own life, which are often entertaining, although the same points are sometimes made more than once. A firmer editor might have reduced the book by a third without losing anything essential.

The Empty Hour is not the last word on its subject, and specialists will find much to argue with. But it raises questions that deserve to be asked, at a time when the opportunity to be bored is disappearing from many people's lives. It is well worth reading, ideally slowly, and without checking your phone between chapters.

Keeping the old, building the new

In cities across the world, few planning decisions provoke as much anger as the fate of old buildings. When a developer proposes to demolish a Victorian warehouse or a row of early twentieth-century shops, there is almost always a campaign to save them. Equally, when a valuable site remains empty because an old building on it is protected, there are complaints that conservation is standing in the way of progress, and in particular of the new homes that many cities badly need. Both sides tend to present the question as a simple choice between keeping and demolishing. I want to argue that this framing is unhelpful, and that the most sensible answer usually lies somewhere in between.

The case for conservation is familiar, and much of it is persuasive. Old buildings are a physical record of a place's history. They show how people lived and worked, and they give a neighbourhood a character that is hard to create from scratch. They also attract visitors, and many towns depend on tourism for a significant part of their income. There is evidence, too, that people value familiar surroundings more than planners sometimes assume: surveys regularly find that residents rank the appearance of their streets among the things that matter most to them about where they live, alongside safety and access to services. Above all, once a building has gone, it has gone for ever. A decision to demolish cannot be reversed, whereas a decision to keep a building can always be reconsidered later.

There is, however, a further argument for keeping old buildings that is often overlooked, and it concerns the environment. Constructing a new building requires enormous quantities of materials such as concrete, steel and glass, and producing these releases large amounts of carbon dioxide. This 'embodied carbon' is released before anyone has moved in, and studies suggest that even a highly energy-efficient new building may take several decades to make up for it through lower energy use. For this reason, some architects have adopted the slogan 'the greenest building is the one that already exists'. The slogan is broadly correct, but it needs to be qualified. Some old buildings are so poorly insulated, and so expensive to heat, that replacing them may well be the better option over the long term. Each case has to be judged on its own merits.

Critics of conservation are right to point out that the rules can be applied too rigidly. In some places, owners of protected buildings are not permitted to replace single-glazed windows, install solar panels or make even minor changes to the interior, which makes the buildings uncomfortable to live in and expensive to maintain. Applications for permission can take many months, and the specialist materials and craftsmen required are often in short supply. Rules of this kind can be self-defeating: if a building cannot be adapted to modern needs, nobody will want to use it, and an empty building is far more likely to fall into disrepair than one that is occupied. Conservation that prevents a building from being used is not really conservation at all.

The most promising solution, in my view, is what is known as adaptive reuse: giving an old building a new function while keeping as much of its original structure as possible. Former factories have been converted into flats, disused churches into libraries and concert halls, and old railway stations into museums. Such projects are not always cheaper than building from new, since old structures often contain unexpected problems, but they combine the environmental benefits of keeping existing materials with the social benefits of creating spaces that people actually need.

Adaptive reuse can, however, be taken too far. In some developments, only the front wall of a historic building is retained, while everything behind it is demolished and replaced by a modern structure. This practice, sometimes called façadism, allows developers to claim that they have respected the past, but in reality it preserves little more than a decorative screen. It keeps the appearance of history while throwing away its substance, and it should be seen for what it is.

There is also the question of who decides which buildings are worth keeping. Traditionally, this has been a matter for experts, who assess buildings according to their age, their architectural quality and their historical importance. This expertise is valuable, but it can overlook the significance that ordinary buildings have for the people who live near them. A local cinema, a corner shop or a school may have little architectural merit, yet it may be central to a community's sense of itself. I believe that such attachments deserve to be taken seriously, and that residents should have a greater say in decisions about their own neighbourhoods than they do at present, even if experts must still play a central role.

None of this makes the decisions easy. There will always be cases where the need for new homes outweighs the value of an old building, and cases where a building is so important that it must be kept whatever the cost. But if we stopped asking whether a building should be kept or demolished, and asked instead how it could be made useful, many of the bitter arguments that surround these decisions might become rather more productive.
